title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
An AI music generation system was trained on copyrighted recordings without authorization from the copyright holders. Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group both sued Udio over this use of their catalogs. The failure occurred during model development, where the system's training data was sourced without the licensing agreements that would later be required to deploy the system lawfully. Catching this would have required either obtaining licenses before training or auditing training data sources against copyright registries before deployment.

The system was deployed to millions of users while operating in legal violation. Udio later settled with Universal and Warner by agreeing to build a new licensed platform, but Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging the same violation involving over 30,000 recordings. A court declined to add all of Sony's claimed recordings to its case, though the scope of the dispute remains contested through ongoing litigation.

Whether Udio intentionally copied specific songs to create similar outputs, or whether the system merely learned patterns from training data that resulted in similar compositions, is not established by the reports.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music. The settlement marks the first major licensing deal between Udio and a major record label, though the financial terms were not disclosed. UMG had previously sued Udio for allegedly using hit songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar melodies without permission or compensation.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, creates original music from text prompts using artificial intelligence. The company has millions of users and significant backing from investors including will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. Under the new licensing agreement, artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. Separately, UMG also announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
